title: The Sustainable Development Goals
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the most ambitious plan in human history -- the 17 Sustainable Development Goals -- and the mixed reality of progress as the 2030 deadline approaches.
competenceGoals: describe the UN Sustainable Development Goals and their purpose
evaluate progress toward achieving the SDGs
discuss the interconnections between different development challenges

content.content:
## A plan for the whole planet

In September 2015, something remarkable happened: all 193 member states of the United Nations agreed on a single shared plan for the future of the world. The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, with its 17 **Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)** and 169 specific targets, is the most ambitious global development plan in history. It covers everything from ending poverty to combating climate change to building peace and justice.

What makes the SDGs different is their reach. Unlike the earlier Millennium Development Goals, which focused mainly on poor countries, the SDGs apply to *all* nations -- rich and poor alike. Norway has committed to achieving them both at home and through international cooperation. They represent the world's shared vision, which is why understanding them is essential for any serious discussion of global challenges and solutions.

## Seventeen goals, five great themes

The 17 goals are often grouped into five broad areas, the "5 Ps": People, Prosperity, Planet, Peace and Partnership. Under **People** come ending poverty (Goal 1), zero hunger (2), good health and well-being (3), quality education (4) and gender equality (5). Under **Prosperity** come clean water and sanitation (6), affordable and clean energy (7), decent work and economic growth (8), industry, innovation and infrastructure (9), and reduced inequalities (10). Under **Planet** come sustainable cities (11), responsible consumption and production (12), climate action (13), life below water (14) and life on land (15). And under **Peace and Partnership** come peace, justice and strong institutions (16) and partnerships for the goals (17).

The SDGs marked a real shift from their predecessors, the Millennium Development Goals which ran from 2000 to 2015. Where the MDGs had 8 goals, the SDGs have 17; where the MDGs focused on developing countries, the SDGs are universal; and the SDGs add environmental sustainability, inequality and governance, developed through a far more inclusive process involving governments, civil society and the private sector. A defining feature is that the goals are deeply *interconnected*. Progress on one often supports progress on others -- educating girls, for instance, improves health, reduces poverty and advances gender equality all at once -- though trade-offs can also occur, as when rapid economic growth strains the environment. Seeing these connections is key to understanding why the goals were designed as a single integrated agenda rather than a list of separate wishes.

The SDGs focus only on developing countries

People, Prosperity, Planet, Peace and Partnership

Only one goal can be achieved at a time
Progress on one goal often supports progress on others
They contradict one another

questions.solution: The goals are interconnected: progress on one, such as education, often advances others like health, poverty reduction and gender equality, though trade-offs can occur.

content.content:
## Progress, setbacks and a looming deadline

With 2030 approaching, the honest assessment of progress is genuinely mixed, and a balanced account records both the gains and the setbacks. There has been real progress in important areas. Global extreme poverty fell from 36 percent in 1990 to around 9 percent by 2023, though it slowed after 2020. Child mortality dropped from 12.7 million deaths in 1990 to roughly 5 million in 2022. Primary school enrolment has passed 90 percent globally. Renewable energy is the fastest-growing energy source, with solar costs falling 90 percent since 2010, and access to electricity rose from 83 to 91 percent of the global population between 2010 and 2022.

But progress has stalled or reversed elsewhere. Global hunger has risen since 2019, affecting around 735 million people, worsened by COVID-19, the war in Ukraine and climate change. Greenhouse gas emissions keep rising, and the world is not on track to limit warming to 1.5 degrees. Species extinction is accelerating, inequality between the richest and poorest countries has widened, and the number of displaced people has reached record levels of over 110 million. The major obstacles are clear: the COVID-19 pandemic reversed years of progress, climate change threatens food and water security, geopolitical conflict disrupts global supplies, there is a financing gap of an estimated 4 trillion US dollars per year, and many governments have not fully integrated the goals into national policy. The UN has warned that, at current rates, the world will not meet most of the 169 targets by 2030, and a "rescue plan" of accelerated action and increased funding has been proposed, though its implementation remains uncertain. Norway's role spans both domestic implementation and significant international support through aid and diplomacy.

content.content:
## In short

The 17 Sustainable Development Goals, adopted by all 193 UN member states in 2015, form the most comprehensive plan ever for tackling poverty, inequality, climate change and governance by 2030. Organised around the 5 Ps -- People, Prosperity, Planet, Peace and Partnership -- they are universal, applying to all countries, and deeply interconnected, so progress on one often supports others. The honest picture of progress is mixed: real gains in poverty reduction, child mortality and clean energy sit alongside setbacks in hunger, climate, biodiversity and inequality. Major obstacles include the pandemic, conflict and a vast financing gap, and the UN has warned most targets will be missed at current rates. Norway contributes both at home and through international aid and diplomacy.
